I've been farming this same land in Quzhou my whole life. My father grew wheat and maize here, and so do I. That's just how it works on the North China Plain — winter wheat goes in October, you harvest it in June, then you immediately plant summer maize on the same land, harvest in October. Double crop, same field. I have about 12 mu.

I don't think much about changing crops. Cotton prices have been bad, and vegetables need more labor and water than I can manage alone. Wheat and maize — I know how to do it, the market is stable enough, and I can sell to the grain station. My son is in the city, so I manage it mostly myself with some hired help at harvest.

For wheat I'll use 济麦22 or 矮抗58 — whatever the seed station has. These improved varieties give better yield than the old stuff and they hold up against disease. I'll rotary-till in September, apply base fertilizer, then plant. I'll irrigate before winter sets in, then again at jointing, and at heading — maybe a fourth time if it's dry during grain fill. I spray once for weeds in early spring, and once for aphids and powdery mildew. That's the usual.

For maize I go straight into the field after wheat harvest. I rent the combine that handles straw chopping and spreading so I don't have to burn. I do rotary tillage to work the straw in, then plant hybrid seed — 郑单958 is what most people around here use. Summer gets rain so I only irrigate once or twice. I top-dress at the big bell stage when the plant really needs nitrogen. One spray for corn borer is usually enough.

I know people say we use too much fertilizer and water. Maybe. But I'm not going to risk a bad yield. I have loans.
